hook: the Nazis take power, and German Jews begin to lose jobs and rights, one rule at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was just having a Tuesday: whole communities, with their bakeries and arguments and weddings. Did you find a face in an old photo? Hold onto it today, gently. Go slowly, and stop whenever you need. Day one thousand seven.

Before any fire, there was paper. A teacher in a German city opens an official letter: his post is ended. Across town, a shopkeeper unlocks his door in the morning and finds a man in uniform standing outside it, next to a painted sign telling customers not to buy from Jews. A lawyer is told he can no longer appear in court. Nothing has been burned yet. It is signs, letters, forms, stamps. Paper. Today's title is a year, and this is what it looked like from the inside: 1933.
screen: `A LETTER ENDING A JOB.` → `A SIGN OUTSIDE THE SHOP.` → `PAPER, NOT FIRE. NOT YET.`

segments.voice: In 1933 the Nazi party came to power in Germany. What came first was not violence on every street. It was rules. That spring there was a national boycott of Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers, with uniformed men posted at the doors. Then a law pushed Jewish officials out of government service: judges, teachers, clerks. Rules limited how many Jewish students schools would take. Books by Jewish writers, and by others the regime disliked, were thrown onto bonfires in public squares. Step by step, much of it was printed, signed and stamped, and each step was a little smaller than the shock it should have caused. That is part of what makes this year hard to read. People woke up each morning in the same house, on the same street, with one thing fewer. The Torah has a line that runs straight against all of it. "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born." One law. The same rights for the person who belongs and the person who arrives. What began in Germany in 1933 was the opposite: one law for some citizens and another for their Jewish neighbors, who had been citizens too. Families had to decide what this meant, with no way of seeing ahead. Some left. Some stayed, hoping it would pass. Reading it now, we know what came next. They didn't. That is why today's line is quiet and plain: rights can be taken. Not only by armies, but by paper, one rule at a time, while ordinary life goes on around it.
screen: `FIRST CAME RULES.` · `A BOYCOTT, A DISMISSAL, A BONFIRE.` · `ONE LAW FOR ALL, SAYS THE TORAH.` · `NO WAY TO SEE AHEAD.` · then, large: `ONE MANNER OF LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: notice one right you have. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one right you rarely think about. To go to school. To keep your job. To walk into any shop. To pray in your own way, or not at all. To vote. Choose one, and hold it for a while. Notice who and what keeps it in place for you: a law, a court, the neighbors who would object if it were taken. If your mind turns to the families of 1933, let it, and then come back to your breath. Rest here until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Boycott. The national campaign in 1933 against Jewish shops, doctors and lawyers that opened the door to law after law stripping Jews of their rights. Today's word.
Your line: rights can be taken. Today, when you use a right without thinking, a vote, a seat in a class, an open door, notice it once. Day one thousand seven.

howItsDone: Jewish communities, schools and Holocaust museums teach the years before the war as part of the story, some by reading the laws and decrees of the time alongside the stories of families who lived under them.

fork.setup: it's 1933 in Germany. the new regime wants to push Jews out of public life. how does it start?
options: with violence on every street at once.
with a string of signs, boycotts and laws, one after another.
with nothing written down at all.
fork.reveal: it began on paper: a boycott, a law ending Jewish officials' jobs, limits on students, books on bonfires. each step was smaller than the shock it should have caused.

trapdoor: what you thought: 1933 is a date in a history book.
what it means: the year the Nazis came to power in Germany and Jews' rights began to be taken by law.
what a scholar hears: how much was done on paper first, a boycott, dismissals, quotas, before the violence came.
